abstract: "Metascientific research has revealed that researchers often fall short in implementing best research practices when designing studies, reporting findings, citing the literature, or sharing data and code. Researchers have time constraints that limit the extent to which they can master all aspects of the research process, and cognitive constraints that limit which practices they remember to implement in their work. By capturing expert knowledge within an automated tool, we aim to elevate the quality of scientific research and disseminate best practices more widely. We illustrate how best practices can be automatically detected by analyzing papers published in Psychological Science in the last decade. Researchers can use the tool before submitting or when reviewing scientific articles. Our module based software tool can easily be extended by experts in the scientific community to automatically check best practices, educate scientists, and increase the quality of scientific reporting."

# Introduction

Metascientific research demonstrates significant room for improvement in how scientists design studies, report findings, and implement open science practices when sharing their work. The uptake of best practices is slow [@sharpe2013resistance], and often suboptimal. For example, researchers often use invalid and unreliable measures [@goos2024assessing], misinterpret non-significant results [@aczel2018quantifying], write insufficiently specific preregistrations [@van2024potential], make mistakes in power analyses [@thibault2024evaluation], and misuse Bayes factors [@tendeiro2024diagnosing]. Although it is the responsibility of scientists to keep up to date on best practices, time constraints and the rapid pace of new developments make this challenging. Peer reviewers, similarly pressed for time, may not identify the absence of best practices. Checklists could potentially increase the adoption of best practices, but in practice they have limited impact, as researchers might not be aware of the existence of checklists, and they still need sufficient expertise to evaluate whether they have adhered to items on the checklist [@dexter2017narrative].

Human factors research suggests that automation (where researchers are kept in the loop) can offer a partial solution. Two recent developments have increased the possibility that best practices can be automatically detected. First, metascientific research has identified where the adoption of best practices is lagging, and offered concrete suggestions for improvement. This work often includes data that can be used as ground truth to validate automated checks. Second, advances in machine learning and artificial intelligence have made it easier to deal with written text, both when turning scientific articles into structured data files (e.g., the GROBID machine learning library), as when extracting or classifying information in written text. This has made it possible to develop algorithms that automatically emulate what experts do when they examine if best practices are present or absent. For example, a reviewer might search for the section in the paper that describes an a-priori power analysis, and then check if people follow best practices, and report the alpha level, desired power, the effect size metric, and a justification for the effect size, for each hypothesis tested [@lakens_justification_2022]. If any of this information is missing, authors should be made aware that they are not following best practices, so that they can improve their paper. While many automated checks for best practices will require only simple text matching based on regular expression, more complex text extraction is possible by using large language models (LLMs).

In this article we introduce a new tool, Metacheck, which uses text search, code, and large language models to extract information from scientific text (which could be a draft of a manuscript, submitted or published articles, or preregistration documents) and provide automated suggestions for improvement. Metacheck is inspired by quality control processes in software development. For example, R package developers run a set of automated checks before they submit their package to the Comprehensive R Archive Network (CRAN). The automated checks aim to identify any remaining issues, and inform developers about how to fix them. The goal of Metacheck is to screen scientific manuscripts, identify areas for improvement based on algorithms that emulate what experts would do while checking a research paper, and educate researchers on how to incorporate best practices. The tool is module based, with a dedicated module for any practice that the community wants to improve, and where automation offers a solution. This means the tool can be extended by the scientific community to fit their needs, and specialised modules can be created for different scientific fields based on what is considered a best practice in that research area. The tool can reduce the burden on peer reviewers by resolving common problems before submission, allowing peer reviewers to focus on those issues that can not be automatically detected.

Automated checks can quite accurately identify the presence or absence of information that should be reported (e.g., is the desired level of power reported in an a-priori power analysis), but a bigger challenge is to evaluate whether the provided information is valid (e.g., is there a good justification for the effect size entered in an a-priori power analysis). Metacheck focuses on the first task, and leaves the evaluation to the user. We will illustrate the potential of automated checks to improve best practices in 4 areas, namely 1) experimental design, 2) open science practices, 3) statistical inferences, and 4) reporting guidelines. Finally, we will demonstrate the usefulness of a tool that can efficiently process text in scientific articles to perform menial tasks (e.g., check if if hyperlinks are working), more easily code information from scientific articles for meta-scientific research, and incorporate existing automated checks (e.g., statcheck, checking if retracted articles are cited) in a single module-based workflow that can be expanded by the scientific community. We perform these checks on all articles published in Psychological Science from 2004 to 2014, which published articles from all subfields in psychology. 

## Use Cases

The current version of Metacheck has two contexts of use. The first use-case is by scientists -- either authors or reviewers -- who have the goal to improve a scientific manuscript by checking for the presence or absence of specific practices. Metacheck can provide recommendations that improve the manuscript in situations where 1) a practice is not sufficiently salient to the scientist to be noticed without assistance, 2) the scientist is not yet able to identify the absence of a practice manually due to a lack of knowledge or training, or 3) scientists do not have time to identify the practice manually. Scientists using Metacheck are aware that all modules make recommendations that can be Type 1 and Type 2 errors. This means that it is possible that many possibly problematic practices are automatically identified, while none are actually problematic upon closer inspection. It is also possible that no problematic practices are found, but many are present.

As developers, our priority is to develop modules with error rates that are low enough to not impact the usability of Metacheck for individual authors, which - following the ISO 9241-11 definition - means "the extent to which a product can be used by specified users to achieve specified goals with effectiveness, efficiency, and satisfaction in a specified context of use". Our working assumption is that preparing a scientific manuscript takes a considerable amount of time, and that scientists care about the quality of their work. Under this assumption, we believe that a tool with high error rates - say up to 50% - will be considered sufficiently useful to be adopted as long as it accurately identified some bad practices that researchers would not have identified themselves. For example, a spelling checker that marks 'Metacheck' and 'manuscirpt' as words with spelling errors, and does not mark 'extend' as a spelling error where the correct word would have been 'extent' remains useful as long as it takes relatively little time to evaluate the suggestions, even though the error rate is 2 out of 3.

The second use-case of Metacheck is as a tool to examine a large number of scientific articles. For example, a university or science funder might be interested in how many manuscripts by researchers that they employ or fund share data and code if this is in line with their policies. A meta-scientist might be interested in how many articles report effect sizes in a specific literature, and test whether there is an improvement in best practices. A scientific journal might want to evaluate how a change in editorial practices has impacted the diversity in populations that are examined in the studies they publish. Metacheck modules can easily be run on large numbers of papers, facilitating text searches and the automatic extraction and classification of information. In this use-case the usability of an automated tool requires low error rates if users want to use the output of the tool. Here, Type 2 errors are problematic, and difficult to identify, as it requires users to manually screen all papers for instances that were missed by the algorithms, and if manual screening was possible, there was no need for an automated tool. Type 1 errors might be easier to identify, but still require manually checking all instances flagged by a module. Therefore, low error rates are important for the usability of Metacheck as a meta-scientific tool. Validation procedures that quantify error rates are essential to safeguard the accuracy of results, and allow users to evaluate whether modules are accurate enough for their purposes, and communicate the error rates when presenting results. It is possible that a module has low-enough error rates for the individual use-case, while error rates are too high for meta-scientific use-cases.

# Examples

## Modules

### Automatically Checking Journal Article Reporting Standards

The journal article reporting standards (JARS) developed by the American Psychological Association (APA) offer guidance on the information that should be reported in scientific articles to enhance their scientific rigour (Appelbaum et al. 2018). Almost every published article would improve if researchers diligently followed JARS. However, the guidelines are not widely known, rarely implemented by authors, and almost never checked by editors or reviewers. Manually checking whether all reporting standards are implemented would be effortful. Automation can help by automatically checking if recommendations are followed. The first reporting guideline that has been implemented in Metacheck is to report exact p-values. The APA Manual states:

> Report exact p values (e.g., p = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report p values less than .001 as p \< .001.

Access to precisely reported p-values allows readers to include the test results in p value meta-analytic tests, such as p-curve, or z-curve (Simonsohn, Nelson, and Simmons 2014; Bartoš and Schimmack 2020), and makes it possible to the check the internal coherence of the reported results with tools such as Statcheck (Nuijten et al. 2015). Metacheck has a dedicated module, `exact_p`, to identify the presence of imprecise p-values. It will return all instances of imprecisely reported p-values in a paper.

We can also examine the difference between significant and non-significant effects, out of interest, and which imprecise p-values are reported. This illustrates how Metacheck makes it possible to easily explore larger numbers of papers, and their properties. This allows us to uncover interesting explorative findings, such as the fact that there is a large peak at p \> 0.25, as it is apparently common for researchers to use this cut-off to indicate a non-significant result. It is unclear to us where this shared practice originates.

```{r}
res_imprecise <- module_run(xml, "exact_p")

res_imprecise$table$significance <- ifelse((res_imprecise$table$p_comp == "<"), "significant", "nonsignificant")

merged_data <- res_imprecise$table %>%
  group_by(id, significance) %>%
  summarise(
    imprecise_text = list(text),  # Store as a list (vector)
    total_imprecise = n(),        # Count number of entries
    .groups = "drop"              # Removes grouping in output
  )

# Rename only the specific columns in merged_data to avoid conflicts during the merge
significant_data <- merged_data %>%
  filter(significance == "significant") %>%
  rename(
    imprecise_text_significant = imprecise_text,
    total_imprecise_significant = total_imprecise
  )

nonsignificant_data <- merged_data %>%
  filter(significance == "nonsignificant") %>%
  rename(
    imprecise_text_nonsignificant = imprecise_text,
    total_imprecise_nonsignificant = total_imprecise
  )

# Merge each subset with psych_science
psych_science <- psych_science %>%
  left_join(significant_data[, c("id", "imprecise_text_significant", "total_imprecise_significant")], by = c("id" = "id"))

psych_science <- psych_science %>%
  left_join(nonsignificant_data[, c("id", "imprecise_text_nonsignificant", "total_imprecise_nonsignificant")], by = c("id" = "id"))

# Calculate percentage of papers with at least one 'total_marginal' per year
summary_df_nonsig <- psych_science %>%
  group_by(year) %>%
  summarise(
    total_papers = n(),
    papers_with_imprecise = sum(total_imprecise_nonsignificant > 0, na.rm = TRUE),
    percentage = (papers_with_imprecise / total_papers) * 100
  )

# Calculate percentage of papers with at least one 'total_marginal' per year
summary_df_sig <- psych_science %>%
  group_by(year) %>%
  summarise(
    total_papers = n(),
    papers_with_imprecise = sum(total_imprecise_significant > 0, na.rm = TRUE),
    percentage = (papers_with_imprecise / total_papers) * 100
  )

# Create grouped bar plot

The peak at 0.25 is due to the tendency of authors to treat *p* values \> 0.25 as an indication of an absence of an effect. It is unclear where this criterion comes from. A possible origin might be the proposed alpha of 0.25 $\le$ $\alpha$ $\le$ 0.35 for stopping rules in forward stepwise selection procedures [@bendel1977comparison], later popularized as $\alpha$ $\le$ .025 in a widely used textbook on logistic regression [@hosmer2013applied], but we are unsure about this. The correct approach to conclude meaningful effects are absent is by performing an equivalence test against a smallest effect size of interest [@lakens_equivalence_2018]. We have also created a related module that simply checks if nonsignificant p values are reported in an article. If so, the module warns researchers against misinterpretations of non-significant results, and provides all sentences with non-singificant results to enable researchers to quickly check for any mistakes. 

```{r}
# The paper below is a good example of the incorrect interpretation of non-significant results. 
paper <- xml$`09567976241268630`
res_nonsig <- metacheck::module_run(paper, "nonsig")
# For example
res_nonsig$table[2,]$expanded
```

### Reporting effect sizes

A second JARS guideline that can be automatically checked is whether people report effect sizes alongside their test result. Each test (e.g., a *t*-test, *F*-test, etc.) should include the corresponding effect size (e.g., a Cohen's *d*, or partial eta-squared). Based on a text search that uses regular expressions (regex), we can identify *t*-tests and *F*-tests that are not followed by an effect size, and warn researchers accordingly.

We have manually checked the *t*-tests and *F*-tests in 250 papers in Psychological Science, and our `effect_size` module detected 100% of *t*-tests with effect sizes, 99% of *t*-tests without effect sizes, 99% of *F*-tests with effect sizes, and 100% of *F*-tests without effect sizes. This is accurate enough to use the module for meta-scientific research, such as examining whether there is an increase in the best practice to report effect sizes for *t*-tests and *F*-tests over time. In the plot below we have run the module on 1838 published articles in the journal Psychological Science between 2014 and 2024. We can see that where a decade ago, around 25% of articles report *t*-tests or *F*-tests without an effect size this has dropped to between 10% and 15% a decade later. Perhaps a tool like Metacheck can reduce this percentage even further.

```{r}
res_effect_size <- module_run(xml, "effect_size")

psych_science <- psych_science %>%
  left_join(res_effect_size$summary)

# combined plot
# Summarise t-tests without effect sizes
summary_t <- psych_science %>%
  group_by(year) %>%
  summarise(
    total_papers = n(),
    papers_with_no_es = sum(ttests_without_es > 0, na.rm = TRUE),
    percentage = (papers_with_no_es / total_papers) * 100
  ) %>%
  mutate(test_type = "t-test")

# Summarise F-tests without effect sizes
summary_f <- psych_science %>%
  group_by(year) %>%
  summarise(
    total_papers = n(),
    papers_with_no_es = sum(Ftests_without_es > 0, na.rm = TRUE),
    percentage = (papers_with_no_es / total_papers) * 100
  ) %>%
  mutate(test_type = "F-test")

# Combine both summaries
combined_summary <- bind_rows(summary_t, summary_f)

# Create grouped bar plot
ggplot(combined_summary, aes(x = factor(year), y = percentage, fill = test_type)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", position = "dodge", color = "black") +
  labs(title = "Papers with t-tests or F-tests Without Effect Sizes",
       x = "Year",
       y = "Percentage of Papers (%)",
       fill = "Test Type") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("t-test" = "skyblue", "F-test" = "orange")) +
  theme_minimal()

```

### Checking Data and Code in Repositories

There is widespread support among scientists for open science practices, such as data and code sharing [@ferguson2023survey]. Funders increasingly require the researchers they fund to make data and code available alongside publications from funded projects. As data and code sharing is a relatively new practice, and there is a lack of training in data management, it is common to see badly documented data repositories. Data repositories would improve substantially if more scientists followed best practices, such as the TIER protocol (https://www.projecttier.org/tier-protocol/protocol-4-0/). By automatically checking data repositories, Metacheck can increase awareness of best practices, and make suggestions for improvements.

At a minimum a data repository for a scientific paper should contain a Read Me file that contains instructions on how to reproduce reported results. If data is shared, it should be stored in a 'data' folder, or at least have the word 'data' in the filename. Furthermore, there should be a codebook or data dictionary that explains which variables are included in the dataset, and what the values mean, in order for others to re-use the data. Code or scripts should similarly be shared in 'code' folder, or at least have the word 'code' in the filename. Ideally peer reviewers or editors would check the contents of a data repository. In practice, time constraints make it so that data repositories are often not checked. Automation can perform some checks of whether data repositories are organized following best practices, reducing the workload of peer reviewers.

We will illustrate the process of checking a data repository by focusing on repositories on the Open Science Framework (www.osf.io). We start by searching for OSF URLs using the `osf_links` function. The function try to extract OSF links as reliably as possible, and detects X out of Y manually coded OSF links in validation datasets [DESCRIBE].

```{r search_osf}
links <- osf_links(xml)
```

If valid, the link is processed, and the OSF Application Programming Interface (API) is used to retrieve whether the link points to a file, project, or registration. This is achieved through the `osf_retrieve()` function. This function will retrieve all child components, files and folders if the argument `recursive = TRUE` is specified, and if the argument `find_project = TRUE` is specified, it will also look up the parent project of any links.

```{r osf_retrieve}
# osf_api_calls()
# osf_delay(delay = 2)
# info <- osf_retrieve(links, recursive = TRUE, find_project = TRUE)
# saveRDS(info, file = "all_osf_file_info_psych_science.rds")
```

We can then use this information to determine if, for each file, the information about the files contains text that makes it easy to determine what is being shared. A simple regular expression text search for 'README', 'codebook', 'script', and 'data' (in a number of possible ways that these words can be written) is used to automatically detect what is shared. # Count occurrences of each osf_id
id_counts <- table(unique_files$osf_id)

# Get osf_ids that appear more than once

So far we have used Metacheck to check whether links exist, are publicly available, and whether certain types of files exist. But it is also possible to automatically download files, examine their contents, and provide feedback to users. This can be useful to examine datasets (e.g., is personal information such as IP addresses included), or code files. Metacheck also contains a function `osf_file_download` to download all files from a project on the OSF while maintaining the folder structure. This function can be used to easily download and check content shared on the OSF. 

It is also possible to download files from data repositories, and perform checks on the content of these files. As an example, we have created a function that will examine four best practices in files that contain R code. These best practices are providing sufficient comments in the code file (so that other users can understand the code), not declaring all libraries in one block at the top of the file (which makes it more cumbersome to install all required R packages), using fixed file paths (which need to be manually changed to make the code run), and not making all files that should be loaded or sourced - such as data files, or other R files with functions - available in the same repository.

# Helper to extract quoted strings (excludes URLs)
extract_quoted <- function(x) {
  qs <- unlist(regmatches(x, gregexpr("(['\"]).*?\\1", x, perl = TRUE)))
  if (length(qs) == 0) return(character(0))
  qs <- gsub("^['\"]|['\"]$", "", qs)
  qs <- qs[!grepl("^https?://", qs, perl = TRUE)]  # exclude URLs
  qs
}

      percent_comments <- (comment_lines / total_lines) * 100
      r_files_only$percentage_comment[i] <- percent_comments

### Checking Preregistrations

It is increasingly common for researchers to preregister their studies [@spitzer2023registered; @imai2025pre]. As preregistration is a new practice, best practices are continuously being developed. Researchers who preregister should ideally continuously stay up-to-date about these best practices, but in practice researchers might not have the time to do so. Automation can assist researchers in keeping up-to-date about updated best practices. 

It has recently become clear that researchers often fail to disclose deviations from their preregistration [@van2024potential], but that is is important to do so. Reviewers could check whether researchers adhere to the preregistration, but this requires additional time. As peer review is already considered insufficiently rewarded, and it is increasingly difficult to find researchers willing to peer review articles, it would be beneficial make such checks as effortless as possible. Here we demonstrate how Metacheck can automatically retrieve the content of a preregistration. The preregistration can then be presented alongside the relevant information in the manuscript. We focus on AsPredicted preregistrations as their structured format makes it especially easy to retrieve information, but the same principle can be applied to other preregistration databases.


```{r}
# As Predicted Links
paper <- psychsci[["09567976241239935"]]
links_ap <- aspredicted_links(psychsci)
ap_url <- links_ap
info_ap <- aspredicted_retrieve(ap_url, id_col = 1, wait = 20)
info_ap$AP_sample_size

```


The first step is to identify hyperlinks to AsPredicted preregistrations. Metacheck provides a convenient function for extracting these links: `aspredicted_links()`. The function cleans up the links when they are incorrectly formatted, such as a link is split across two sentences, which is common in scientific PDF files. The published version of articles sometimes still includes 'blind' links, which are useful to allow anonymous peer review, but when a paper is accepted, the link should be replaced by the normal link to the AsPredicted preregistration. Forgetting to replace these links is an example of a lapse that automation can prevent. If a link to AsPredicted is identified, the function `aspredicted_retrieve()` can be used to retrieve the preregistration from the AsPredicted website. Each item in the preregistration, such as the planned sample size, is stored. 

Recent metascientific research on preregistrations [@vandenakker_potential_2024] has shown that the most common deviation from a preregistration in practice is that researchers do not collect the sample size that they preregistered. This is not necessarily problematic, as a difference might be only a single datapoint. Nevertheless, researchers should discuss the deviation, and evaluate whether the deviation impacts the severity of the test [@lakens_when_2024]. Checking the sample size of a study against the preregistration requires some effort, as the preregistration document needs to be opened, and the text in the manuscript needs to be located. Recently, a fully automatic comparison tool, ([RegCheck](https://regcheck.app/)) has been created by Jamie Cummins from the University of Bern, that relies on large language models and AI where users upload the manuscript, the preregistration, and receive an automated comparison. We take a slightly different approach. We retrieve the preregistration from AsPredicted automatically, and present users with the information about the preregistered sample size (which is straightforward given the structured approach of the AsPredicted template). We then recommend users to compare this information against the method section in the manuscript.

### Checking Power Analyses

To design an informative study, researchers should collect sufficient data. The final number of observations should be justified respect to the inferential goal of the study [@lakens_justification_2022]. One approach to a sample size justification is an a priori power analysis. If an a priori power analysis is performed, it should be reported transparently for peers to be able to evaluate the sample size justification. This requires researchers to specify the type of power analysis (e.g., a priori, compromise, sensitivity), the statistical test that the power analysis is performed for (e.g., an independent *t*-test, a within-between interaction effect in a 2x2 ANOVA), the effect size metric (e.g., *d*, *r*, odds ratio), the effect size (a numerical value, e.g., 0.3), the desired power (e.g., 95%), and the alpha level (e.g., 0.05). Many power analyses do not transparently report this information. Moreover, some researchers perform post-hoc power analyses where they compute the power for the observed effect size, given the collected sample size, even though this practice is flawed.

The powercheck module aims to assist researchers in fully reporting power analysis, and dissuade them from performing a post-hoc power analysis. It first searches for the word "power\[ed\]", and based on a pre-trained local logistic regression model classifies sentences as a statistical power analysis, or not. Sentences classified as probable power analysis statements are then expanded by including the previous and two subsequent sentences, and sent to Groq, a service for artificial intelligence inference. Groq can run a range of different language models, such as Llama 3.3 70B, an open source language model. Based on a prompt the Groq API returns a JSON structured dataset with either the content of the parameters that should be reported in a power analysis, or missing information if the language model can not retrieve the values for certain parameters.

The information retrieved from the language model is then cleaned (e.g., by removing spaces) and standardized (e.g., Cohen's d, ds, and Hedges' g are all recoded as 'd', 0.8, 80%, and .80 are recoded as 0.80, etc.). An additional simple text search for words such as 'post-hoc power' or 'observed power' is performed. Based on this information users are informed about which parameters were not automatically identified, or why observed power analyses should not be informed. Given the complexity of natural language, we should expect Type 1 and type 2 errors. For an example , the sentence "Null of 33% power Note: The observed p -curve includes 29 statistically significant (p \< .05) results, of which 14 are p \< .025. There were 8 additional results entered but excluded from p-curve because they were p \> .05." was incorrectly classified as a sentence describing a power analysis (i.e., a Type 1 error) dus to the presence of a significance level threshold, and numbers of entities included and excluded in the analysis. The following sentence is an example of a Type 2 error: "We attempted to recruit 200 participants to have sufficient power to detect a small to moderate effect size, but in recruiting groups of friends on campus, we ended up with 199 fluent English speakers (105 female)". This statement provides too minimal information about the details of the power analysis to be classified as one.
Type 1 errors are annoying, but this annoyance is hopefully in the long run compensated by the benefits of a tool such as Metacheck. Type 2 errors miss an opportunity to inform users of best practices. However, it is possible to still report the result of the power module by stating that no reported power analyses were identified, and informing users that if this is incorrect, they might want to reconsider whether the way they reported the power analysis is clear enough for human readers. A statement such as "We performed an a-priori power analysis for a one-sided dependent t-test with an alpha of 0.05, a desired power of 0.95, an effect size of interest of dz = 0.2, which lead to a required sample size of N = 272" should have a very high probability of being automatically detected and should allow all parameters to be automatically retrieved by the algorithm. Out of all 707 power analysis statements (although these include some double counted due to overlapping sentences) 72 were fully reported. Some missing information might not be considered too problematic, such as the alpha level which is almost exclusively 5% (although some researchers used 0.01 or corrected the alpha level for multiple comparisons) or the test (which can sometimes - although too often not - be retrieved from the result section. The simple warning for observed power based simply on a regex text search would catch the use of 'post-hoc' power in 45 instances across 37 papers. This bad practice is a rare occurrence, but flaw is relatively serious, and hence worth correcting through an automated tool.

ADD POWER ANALYSIS EXAMPLE

We should summarize that 1) Not all power analyses are detected, and it is important to increase the accuracy of the workflow. There are false positives and false negatives. At the same time, for the 1838 papers in psych science, we can currently identify and extract information for 445 papers, which contain 707 sentences identified as power analyses. In these 445 we can warn people for missing statistical tests 334 times, missing alpha levels 296 times, missing effect sizes 106 times, missing type of effect sizes 142 times, desired power in 108 papers and the final sample size in XX.

## Creating Metacheck Modules

Metacheck is module based. Modules are very similar to the functions in R packages. Community engagement and epistemic diversity is a core value of the Metacheck developers. A healthy science discusses what should be considered a best practice. We have therefore made it as easy as possible for anyone to transform their own views about best practices into a Metacheck module. Anyone can create a module that performs checks and validate it against ground truth. Modules can be shared and installed locally, or submitted to the Metacheck R package through a pull request on Github. This makes it possible for journals in any scientific discipline to create modules that check requirements in the author submission guidelines, for experts on any aspect of the scientific process to create automated warnings for problems they often have to point out during peer review, and for organizations to create a module that check if researchers adhere to reporting guidelines that they create. 

Metacheck can also function as a hub for existing automated checks. Although researchers run their manuscript through multiple tools, websites, or services, it is more convenient if a single tool combines all existing checks. This might also help researchers to discover automated checks that they are not yet aware of. As a demonstration of how other checks can be incorporated into Metacheck we have created a Statcheck module (Nuijten et al. 2015) for Metacheck. Statcheck has not been extensively validated yet, but an initial study shows `that only for *t*t-tests, *F*-tests, and chi-squared tests in 48 articles in two psychology journals, the true positive rate is 85.3% (which increases to 100% if researchers performing one-tailed tests are indicated by to “one-tailed”, “one-sided”, or “directional” in the article). Statcheck has not been validated for tests of correlations (*r*) or *Z*-tests, and based on anecdotal observations the accuracy for these tests seems much lower. As a core value of Metacheck is to only include validated checks, the Statcheck module of Metacheck will by default not evaluate tests of correlations and *Z*-tests, until the performance of Statcheck on these tests has been validated.

```{r}
statcheck <- metacheck::module_run(xml, "statcheck")
save(statcheck, file = "data/statcheck_results.RData")



```

## Menial tasks

So far we have focused on modules that capture expertise about best practices. There is an additional category of checks that do not require expertise, but still benefit from being automated because this saved time, and researchers might forget to perform these checks. We will illustrates the usefulness of Metacheck to perform such menial tasks through two modules. The `url_check` module checks all hyperlinks in an article and 1) identifies the presence of anonymized links to the Open Science Framework or AsPredicted in articles, and warns to replace them before publication with public links, and 2) checks whether hyperlinks resolve (e.g., whether the website that is linked to loads) and warns researchers to consider linking to a more stable version of the website, such as the Wayback Machine by the Internet Archive.

```{r}
# Random test to get all urls, check if individual are open.
# The result of all URLs is too large and messy to check all.

# To make a module our of this we should also include the OSF view only check, and the aspredicted blind link check. 

all_url <- metacheck::module_run(xml, "all_urls")
all_url <- unique(all_url$table["text"])

filtered_url <- all_url %>%
  mutate(text = str_trim(text)) %>% 
  filter(str_detect(text, regex("^(https?://|www\\.)", ignore_case = TRUE))) %>%
  filter(!coalesce(str_detect(text, regex("osf\\.io|aspredicted|/doi|dx.doi|orcid.org|sagepub|psychologicalscience.org/publications", 
                                          ignore_case = TRUE)), FALSE))

# Can we fix some links, by replacing > . with .? 

# ---- Helper: robust check for a single URL
check_url_live <- function(raw_url, timeout_sec = 5) {
  # trim whitespace
  url <- trimws(raw_url)

  # Return a consistent "failure" object on empty/NA
  if (is.na(url) || identical(url, "")) {
    return(list(ok = FALSE, status = NA_integer_, final_url = NA_character_))
  }

  # Build candidate URLs:
  # - If starts with "www.", try https then http
  # - If already has http/https, use as-is
  # - Otherwise, try both https and http (defensive)
  if (grepl("^www\\.", url, ignore.case = TRUE)) {
    candidates <- c(paste0("https://", url), paste0("http://", url))
  } else if (grepl("^https?://", url, ignore.case = TRUE)) {
    candidates <- c(url)
  } else {
    candidates <- c(paste0("https://", url), paste0("http://", url))
  }

  # Common request config: follow redirects, set UA, set timeout
  ua <- user_agent(
    "Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64) AppleWebKit/537.36 (KHTML, like Gecko) R/httr"
  )
  cfg <- config(followlocation = TRUE)
  to  <- timeout(timeout_sec)

  request_once <- function(u, method = "HEAD") {
    # Return NULL on any network/SSL/DNS error
    res <- tryCatch(
      {
        if (identical(method, "HEAD")) {
          httr::HEAD(u, ua, cfg, to)
        } else {
          httr::GET(u, ua, cfg, to)
        }
      },
      error = function(e) NULL
    )
    if (is.null(res)) return(NULL)
    list(status = httr::status_code(res), final_url = res$url)
  }

  # Try each candidate: HEAD first, then GET fallback
  for (u in candidates) {
    # 1) HEAD (fast; but some servers block or misconfigure it)
    head_res <- request_once(u, "HEAD")
    if (!is.null(head_res) && head_res$status < 400) {
      return(list(ok = TRUE, status = head_res$status, final_url = head_res$final_url))
    }

    # 2) Fallback to GET if HEAD is blocked (405/403) or failed
    need_get <- is.null(head_res) || head_res$status %in% c(405, 403)
    if (need_get) {
      get_res <- request_once(u, "GET")
      if (!is.null(get_res) && get_res$status < 400) {
        return(list(ok = TRUE, status = get_res$status, final_url = get_res$final_url))
      }
    }

    # Otherwise, move to the next candidate (e.g., try http after https)
  }

  # Nothing worked
  list(ok = FALSE, status = NA_integer_, final_url = NA_character_)
}

# Preallocate vectors for speed and clean types
n <- nrow(filtered_url)
checked      <- integer(n)
http_status  <- rep(NA_integer_, n)
resolved_url <- rep(NA_character_, n)

# Loop through rows
for (i in seq_len(n)) {
  res <- check_url_live(filtered_url$text[i], timeout_sec = 5)
  checked[i]      <- if (isTRUE(res$ok)) 1 else 0
  http_status[i]  <- if (is.null(res$status)) NA_integer_ else res$status
  resolved_url[i] <- if (is.null(res$final_url)) NA_character_ else res$final_url

  # (optional) simple progress every 200 rows:
  message("Checked ", i, " / ", n)
}

# Add columns to your tibble
filtered_url$checked      <- checked
filtered_url$http_status  <- http_status
filtered_url$resolved_url <- resolved_url

save(filtered_url, file = "links_down_psych_science.RData")

```

### Check References

The `ref_check` module checks the reference list of scientific articles and 1) warns for missing DOI's in the reference list, and attempts to automatically add them when missing, 2) checks whether articles have corrections, expressions of concern, or are retracted, according to the RetractionWatch, 3) points out when original articles are cited, but direct replication studies of the same paper exist but have not been cited (Röseler, 2024). 

```{r}

# Script to get all references in a single table

# 1) Extract nested data frames
bibs <- lapply(xml, function(x) x$bib)

# 2) Normalize each 'bib' so that 'year' is integer of correct length (even for 0-row dfs)
coerce_year_to_integer <- function(df) {
  # If NULL, replace by an empty data frame
  if (is.null(df)) df <- data.frame()
  
  df <- as.data.frame(df, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  nr <- nrow(df)
  
  # If 'year' is missing, create it with the right length
  if (!"year" %in% names(df)) {
    df$year <- if (nr == 0) integer(0) else rep(NA_integer_, nr)
    return(df)
  }
  
  # Coerce to character first, then to integer
  y_chr <- as.character(df$year)
  y_int <- suppressWarnings(as.integer(y_chr))
  
  # For non-numeric forms, try to extract a 4-digit year
  need_extract <- is.na(y_int) & !is.na(y_chr) & nzchar(y_chr)
  if (any(need_extract)) {
    m   <- regexpr("\\b\\d{4}\\b", y_chr[need_extract])
    got <- ifelse(m > 0,
                  substring(y_chr[need_extract], m, m + attr(m, "match.length") - 1),
                  NA_character_)
    y_int[need_extract] <- suppressWarnings(as.integer(got))
  }
  
  # Assign back; lengths now match nrow(df), including the 0-row case
  df$year <- y_int
  df
}

bibs_fixed <- lapply(bibs, coerce_year_to_integer)

# Function to get a doi from crossref by sending the full reference text.  
get_doi <- function(reference) {
  options(crossref_email = "d.lakens@tue.nl")
  tryCatch({
    res <- cr_works(query = reference, limit = 1)
    if (nrow(res$data) > 0) {
      return(res$data$doi[1])
    } else {
      return(NA)
    }
  }, error = function(e) {
    return(NA)
  })
}

# Function that takes a DOI, and retrieves information from pubpeer related to post-publication peer review comments. 
get_pubpeer_comment <- function(doi) {
  url <- "https://pubpeer.com/v3/publications?devkey=PubPeerZotero"
  
  body <- list(
    dois = list(tolower(doi))
  )
  
  response <- POST(
    url,
    body = toJSON(body, auto_unbox = TRUE),
    encode = "raw",
    add_headers(`Content-Type` = "application/json;charset=UTF-8")
  )
  
  if (status_code(response) == 200) {
    data <- content(response, as = "parsed", type = "application/json")
    if (length(data[["feedbacks"]]) > 0) {
      return(list(
        total_comments = data[["feedbacks"]][[1]][["total_comments"]],
        url = data[["feedbacks"]][[1]][["url"]],
        users = strsplit(data[["feedbacks"]][[1]][["users"]], ",\\s*")[[1]]
      ))
    } else {
      return(NULL)  # No feedback found
    }
  } else {
    return(NULL)  # Request failed
  }
}

# For example:
# get_pubpeer_comment("10.1037/0022-3514.81.4.657")

# Function that takes the references of a papercheck paper (paper[["bib"]]), adds dois where missing (using the get_doi() function) and refers the table with references, with the following columns added:
# 1: total_comments: Total number of pubpeer comments
# 2: pubpeer_url: Link to read the pubpeer comments. 
# 3: users: NAmes of the people who posted. Mainly used to filter out statcheck comments
# 4: doi_from_crossref: Is the DOI in the dataframe original (extracted by GROBID from the references = 0) or added by crossref (= 1). Both can be inaccurate, but crossref more so. 

# We could add a check for the DOI, by going to the DOI, and check if the website has some info we would expect, like the journal name. 
refs <- all_psych_science_refs
ref_check <- function(paper) {
  # Read in FReD database. 
  # We can also download the latest version https://osf.io/9r62x/files/z5u9b, or add a function to check the latest version and update it if needed. 
  FReD <- read_excel("data/FReD.xlsx")
  # Remove first 2 rows
  FReD <- FReD[-c(1, 2), ]
  # Remove all rows without doi for original study and replication
  FReD <- FReD[FReD$doi_original != "" & !is.na(FReD$doi_original) & 
             FReD$doi_replication != "" & !is.na(FReD$doi_replication), ]
  attr(FReD, "date") <- Sys.Date()

# Keep only the column we need
FReD <- FReD %>%
  select(ref_original, doi_original, ref_replication, doi_replication)


  # Only keep article types in the references. We can't get doi's for other types (books, miscellaneous), and trying will just slow down the function.
  
  refs <- refs %>%
    filter(bibtype == "Article")

  # If there are no rows, return immediately
  if (nrow(refs) == 0) {
    return(refs)
  }
  # Add new columns to refs
  refs$total_comments <- NA_integer_
  refs$pubpeer_url <- NA_character_
  refs$users <- NA_character_
  refs$doi_from_crossref <- NA_character_
  refs$retraction_watch <- NA_character_
  
  # Initialize progress bar
  pb <- txtProgressBar(min = 0, max = nrow(refs), style = 3)
  
  for (i in seq_len(nrow(refs))) {
    # Ensure DOI is present
    if (is.na(refs$doi[i])) {
      doi <- get_doi(refs$ref[i])   # run only if doi is NA
      refs$doi_from_crossref[i] <- 1
      refs$doi[i] <- doi            # replace NA with the new value
    } else {
      doi <- refs$doi[i]
      refs$doi_from_crossref[i] <- 0
    }
    
    feedback <- get_pubpeer_comment(doi)
    
    # Add pubpeer info to columns
    if (!is.null(feedback)) {
      refs$total_comments[i] <- feedback$total_comments
      refs$pubpeer_url[i] <- feedback$url
      refs$users[i] <- paste(feedback$users, collapse = ", ")
    }
    
    setTxtProgressBar(pb, i)
  }
  # This now crashes due to the select doi 
  retraction_table <- refs %>%
    inner_join(
      refs, 
      retractionwatch(), 
      by = 'doi'
      )
  
  
  refs <- refs %>%
  left_join(retraction_table %>% select(doi, retractionwatch), by = "doi", relationship = "many-to-many")


replication_table <- refs %>% select(doi) %>%
  inner_join(
    FReD %>% select(ref_original, doi_original, ref_replication, doi_replication),
    by = c("doi" = "doi_original"),
    relationship = "many-to-many"
  )
  # Some original studies have more than 1 replication in the same paper (e.g., many labs replications), but we just want to point to the dois of papers containing replication studies. 
  replication_table <- replication_table[!duplicated(replication_table["doi_replication"]), ]

  # To be able to add 
  replication_table_collapsed <- replication_table %>%
    group_by(doi) %>%
    summarise(
      ref_replication = paste(ref_replication, collapse = "; "),
      doi_replication = paste(doi_replication, collapse = "; "),
      .groups = "drop"
    )
  
    all_psych_science_refs <- all_psych_science_refs %>%
    left_join(replication_table_collapsed %>% select(doi, ref_replication, doi_replication), by = "doi", relationship = "many-to-many")

  close(pb)
  return(refs)
}

# Discussion

To prevent widespread misuse of an automated tool such as Metacheck, it is important to realize the limits of the tool. Although it might seem desirable to develop modules with high accuracy, a cost-benefit analysis might indicate that at this phase it is more important to invest time to develop 10 modules that assist researchers to check their papers with a relatively high error rate, then to spend the same time on two modules that can be used meta-scientifically with very low error rates. The flexibility of human language combined with the lack of standardization in how researchers report information in scientific manuscripts are such that reducing error rates from 50% to 20% is much easier than reducing error rates from 20% to 5%. Our current approach is to follow the Pareto principle and focus on the 20% of the ways in which researchers get something wrong, that when when identified, would prevent 80% of the times researchers get something wrong.

### Hyperlinks

Many scientific articles link to additional information that is not included in the article, such as open data, materials, and code, a preregistration, or supplementary information. Although it is useful to have access to this information, it can also be cumbersome to retrieve it. Journals lack a systematic way of providing access to information outside of the article, and the additional information that is provided is often not structured well. Although this is expected as science transitions to more transparency, the fact that supplementary information is often not easily findable or accessible limits its use. Automation can assists researchers by making information more readily available.

One starting point to retrieve information is a hyperlink. We can retrieve hyperlinks from pdf articles in two ways. First, GROBID automatically extracts hyperlinks (i.e., text that can be clicked to open an external website). Second, regular expressions can identify hyperlinks that can not be clicked based on common text patterns in hyperlinks (e.g., the presence of http or www, followed by a string of characters). To capture all hyperlinks it is often necessary to iteratively search the text. Text parsing often struggles with hyperlinks, and it is common to see line breaks in hyperlinks that result in hyperlinks being split across two sentences or having spaces in the hyperlink that need to be removed. Identifying and fixing hyperlinks requires knowledge about the structure of hyperlinks (e.g., links to the Open Science Framework or AsPredicted have either 5 or 6 characters after the domain).

We will provide two illustrations of the usefulness of combining domain expertise with automatically detecting hyperlinks. The first example pertains to the presence of links to anonymized files that are used during the peer review process in published articles. Many journals anonymize authors, which requires linking to anonymized supplementary files. This can be achieved on AsPredicted through a special 'blind' link (e.g., https://aspredicted.org/blind.php?x=5tq3pg) or a 'view_only' link to the OSF. Sometimes, these links make it into the published article, even though they should be replaced by the public link after acceptance.

```{r}

down_check <- metacheck:::site_down(all_url$text[175], error = FALSE)

### OSF Links

```{r}
# Define the regular expression pattern for detecting OSF URLs 
# We first find any osf link to fix some not completely caught
RGX_OSF <- "osf\\.io"

          print("root id closed, saving node id")
        })

      text_found$osf_project_id[i] <- osf_project_id[2]
      text_found$osf_type[i] <- "file"
      }
  }

  # Check if it is a registration
  if (is.null(osf_project_id)) {

    osf_project_id <- tryCatch(
      registration <- GET(paste("https://api.osf.io/v2/registrations/?filter[id]=",link, sep = "")),
      error = function(e) {

      })
    registration <- fromJSON(rawToChar(registration$content))
    # Store the results in the data frame
    if (length(registration$data) != 0) {
      print("succes 3")
      description <- registration$data$attributes$title
      parent_project <- registration$data$relationships$registered_from$data$id
        # Get parent project
      parent_node  <- tryCatch(
        GET(paste(registration$data$relationships$registered_from$links$related$href)),
        error = function(e) {
          return(NULL)  # Return null if retrieval fails (but it always gets some data)
        })
      if (!is.null(parent_node)) {
        project <- fromJSON(rawToChar(parent_node$content))
        project_id <- ifelse(is.null(project$data$id), "NA", project$data$id)
        project_title <- ifelse(is.null(project$data$attributes$title), "NA", project$data$attributes$title)
        text_found$osf_project_name[i] <- project_title
        text_found$osf_project_id[i] <- project_id
        text_found$osf_type[i] <- "registration"
      }
    }
    # If the call to get data returns an empty list, it is closed
    if (length(registration$data) == 0) {
      text_found$osf_project_name[i] <- NA
        text_found$osf_project_id[i] <- NA
        text_found$osf_type[i] <- "CLOSED"
      
    }
  }
}

To summarize, in `length(psych_science$doi)` articles published in psychological science we observed `length(text_found$text)` unique view-only links to the OSF. Of these, `sum(text_found$osf_type == "CLOSED")` are not made public. Similarly, we found `length(text_found_as_predicted_blind$text)` unique blind links to AsPredicted, which should have linked to their public counterparts.

Then we can take the preregistrations, and do something with them, similar to Aspredicted below.

```{r}
# Load the dataframe text_found that contains all osf retrieved info.
load(file = "psychscience_osf_full.RData")

# Only select registrations
registration_df <- text_found %>%
  filter(osf_type == "registration")
# Remove double rows
registration_df <- registration_df %>%
  distinct(osf_id, .keep_all = TRUE)  #

categorize_preregistration <- function(prereg_id) {
  
  print("Waiting a second for rate limitations")
  Sys.sleep(5)

  # Step 1: Fetch registration data from the API
  registration <- tryCatch({
    GET(paste0("https://api.osf.io/v2/registrations/?filter[id]=", prereg_id))
  }, error = function(e) {
    print(paste("API request failed for", prereg_id, "-", e$message))
    return(NULL)  # Return NULL to indicate failure
  })
  
  # If API call failed, return an error result
  if (is.null(registration) || registration$status_code != 200) {
    print(paste("Failed to fetch data for", prereg_id, "- HTTP status:", registration$status_code))
    return(list(prereg_id = prereg_id, content = NA, result = "ERROR"))
  }
  
  # Step 3: Parse the JSON content
  registration_content <- tryCatch({
    fromJSON(rawToChar(registration$content))
  }, error = function(e) {
    print(paste("Failed to parse JSON for", prereg_id, "-", e$message))
    return(NULL)
  })

  # If JSON parsing failed, return an error
  if (is.null(registration_content) || !is.list(registration_content) || is.null(registration_content$data)) {
    print(paste("Invalid response structure for", prereg_id))
    return(list(prereg_id = prereg_id, content = NA, result = "ERROR"))
  }
  
  # Step 5: Extract metadata safely
  registered_meta <- registration_content$data$attributes$registered_meta
  if (is.null(registered_meta)) {
    print(paste("No registered_meta found for", prereg_id))
    return(list(prereg_id = prereg_id, content = NA, result = "ERROR"))
  }
  
  # Initialize a list to store rows for the dataframe
  df_rows <- list()

  # Loop through metadata and prepare rows
  for (q in names(registered_meta)) {
    value_entry <- registered_meta[[q]]$value  # Store value reference
    
    # Check if value_entry is a list and has the necessary nested structure
    if (is.list(value_entry) && 
        "question" %in% names(value_entry) && 
        "uploader" %in% names(value_entry) && 
        !is.null(value_entry$question$value) && 
        !is.na(value_entry$question$value)) {
      
      # Extract nested values safely
      question_value <- as.character(value_entry$question$value)
      uploader_value <- as.character(value_entry$uploader$value)
      
      df_rows[[q]] <- data.frame(
        question = q,
        main_value = question_value,
        uploader_value = uploader_value,
        stringsAsFactors = FALSE
      )
      
    } else {
      # Fallback: Extract only the main value if the nested structure is missing
      main_value <- as.character(value_entry)
      
      df_rows[[q]] <- data.frame(
        question = q,
        main_value = main_value,
        uploader_value = NA,  # No uploader value for default cases
        stringsAsFactors = FALSE
      )
    }
  }

  # Combine rows into a single dataframe
  prereg_info_osf <- do.call(rbind, df_rows)

  # Collapse the content of main values
  collapsed_content <- paste(prereg_info_osf$main_value, collapse = " ")

  # Truncate to prevent errors in API call
  max_length <- 2000  # Adjust based on API limits
  collapsed_content <- substr(collapsed_content, 1, max_length)

  # Create the prompt for categorization
  prompt <- "Answer TRUE if the following text refers to a preregistration of a scientific study where researchers describe their hypotheses and planned analyses, or if they text only contains 'NO'. Answer FALSE if this text refers to creating a frozen version of a project related to a publication, indicated by, for example, a reference to the name of a scientific journal. The text is: "

  # Step 6: Send the prompt to the GPT-based API
  response_groq <- tryCatch({
    llm(text = collapsed_content, query = prompt)
  }, error = function(e) {
    print(paste("Failed to get response from GPT API for", prereg_id, "-", e$message))
    return("ERROR")
  })
  
  # Step 7: Extract TRUE or FALSE from the response
  result <- regmatches(response_groq, regexpr("\\b(TRUE|FALSE)\\b", response_groq))
  if (length(result) == 0) result <- "ERROR"  # Handle cases where no valid response is returned
  
  # Return the result as a list
  return(list(
    prereg_id = prereg_id,
    prereg_info_osf = prereg_info_osf,
    content = collapsed_content,
    result = result
  ))
}

prereg_results_list <- lapply(registration_df$osf_id, categorize_preregistration)

  # If neither, return NA
  else {

  }
}))

# We can not send too long text to Groq, so we trim the end. 
trim_text <- function(text, max_chars = 5950) {
  char_count <- nchar(text)/4
  if (char_count > max_chars) {
    message("Text is too long. Trimming to ", max_chars, " characters.")
    text <- substr(text, 1, max_chars)
  }
  return(text)
}

# Initialize empty data frame to store results
all_files_df <- data.frame(
  file_name = character(),

osf_ids_vector <- as.character(all_osf_links_df$osf_project_id) # extract the column
osf_ids_vector <- osf_ids_vector[!(is.na(osf_ids_vector) | osf_ids_vector == "NA")]
osf_ids_vector <- unique(osf_ids_vector)                    # remove duplicates

for (i in 1:length(osf_ids_vector)) {
  link <- as.character(osf_ids_vector[i])  # Get the osf_id
  if (is.na(link) || link == "NA" || link == "") {
    print(paste("Skipping row", i, "- link is NA or empty"))
    next
  }
  
  # print("Waiting a second for rate limitations")
  # Sys.sleep(5)
  
  print(link)
  print(i)
  
  # Wrap all risky calls in tryCatch
  result <- tryCatch({
    osf_id <- as_id(link)  # may error if invalid ID
    osf_project <- osf_retrieve_node(osf_id)
    wiki_link <- GET(osf_project[[3]][[1]][["relationships"]][["wikis"]][["links"]][["related"]][["href"]])
    wiki_info <- fromJSON(rawToChar(wiki_link$content))$data$links$download
    wiki_info <- tail(wiki_info, 1) # take last wiki
    wiki <- if (is.null(wiki_info)) NA else content(GET(wiki_info), as = "text", encoding = "UTF-8")
        
    children_resp <- GET(osf_project[[3]][[1]][["relationships"]][["children"]][["links"]][["related"]][["href"]])
    # If GET returns error status, stop to catch below
    if (http_error(children_resp)) {
      stop(paste("HTTP error", status_code(children_resp)))
    }
    children <- fromJSON(rawToChar(children_resp$content))[["data"]][["id"]]
    
    # Combine osf_project$id with children (if not NULL)
    project_ids <- c(osf_project$id, if (!is.null(children)) children)
    
    pid <- project_ids[1]
    
    for (pid in project_ids) {
      tryCatch({
        project_node <- osf_retrieve_node(pid)
        files <- osf_ls_files(project_node)
        title <- osf_project$name
        if (nrow(files) > 0) {
          temp_df <- data.frame(
            file_name = files$name,
            project_id = pid,
            parent_id = osf_project$id,
            folder_name = project_node$name,
            title = title,
            wiki = wiki,
            stringsAsFactors = FALSE
          )
          all_files_df <<- bind_rows(all_files_df, temp_df)  # use <<- to update outside the tryCatch
        }
      }, error = function(e) {
        # Handle 403/404 inside inner loop
        if (grepl("403|404", e$message)) {
          message(paste("Skipping project ID", pid, "- error:", e$message))
        } else {
          stop(e)  # re-throw other errors
        }
      })
    }
    NULL  # return NULL if all successful
  }, error = function(e) {
    # Catch errors from outer calls (like as_id or osf_retrieve_node for link)
    if (grepl("403|404", e$message)) {
      message(paste("Skipping OSF link", link, "- error:", e$message))
      NULL
    } else {
      stop(e)  # re-throw unexpected errors
    }
  })
}

    cat("There are no R files\n")
  } else {
    # Iterate over each row in osf_files
    for (i in seq_len(nrow(osf_files))) {
      # Read in the R code
      download_link <- osf_files[[3]][[i]][["links"]][["download"]]
      print(download_link)
      
      # Use tryCatch to handle warnings when reading the file
      r_code <- tryCatch(
        readLines(url(download_link)),
        warning = function(w) {
          cat(sprintf("Skipping file due to warning: %s\n", conditionMessage(w)))
          return(NULL)
        },
        error = function(e) {
          cat(sprintf("Skipping file due to error: %s\n", conditionMessage(e)))
          return(NULL)
        }
      )
      
      # Skip further processing if the code is NULL
      if (is.null(r_code)) next

      # Search for absolute file paths (both Windows and Unix)
      absolute_paths <- grep('(["\'])([A-Za-z]:\\\\|/|~)', r_code, value = TRUE)

      # Print the result
      if (length(absolute_paths) > 0) {
        cat("We found the following absolute paths:\n")
        cat(absolute_paths, sep = "\n")
      } else {
        cat("There are no absolute paths, well done!\n")
      }

      # Find lines where libraries are loaded
      library_lines <- grep("\\b(library|require)\\(", r_code)

      # Check if libraries are loaded at multiple places
      if (length(library_lines) > 1 && !all(diff(library_lines) == 1)) {
        cat("Libraries are loaded in multiple places in the script:\n")
        cat(sprintf("Line %d: %s\n", library_lines, r_code[library_lines]), sep = "")
      } else if (length(library_lines) > 0) {
        cat("Libraries are loaded in a single block, well done!\n")
      } else {
        # Warning if no libraries are loaded
        cat("Warning: No libraries are specified in this script.\n")
      }
    }
  }
}

This would be true if the power directly follows statistical test results, or if power is computed for the results observed in the study. Return 'post hoc' if so. If the power analysis is done 'a priori', before data is collected, to determine the sample size of the study, answer 'a priori'. If it is unclear, return 'unclear', and if the statement is not about statistical power, return 'no power analysis'"

res <- llm(testset$text, query)

  "} ",
  "The text is:"
)

# Regular expression pattern to match key-value pairs including "total sample size"
pattern <- "\"(.*?)\":\\s*\"?([^,\n]+)\"?"

# Function to extract key-value pairs from the text
extract_info <- function(text) {
  # Extract key-value pairs using the regex pattern
  matches <- regmatches(text, gregexpr(pattern, text, perl = TRUE))
  
  # Flatten the list of matches
  key_value_pairs <- unlist(matches)
  
  # Check if key_value_pairs is empty
  if(length(key_value_pairs) == 0) {
    return(NULL)
  }
  
  # Extract keys and values separately
  keys <- gsub("\"(.*?)\":.*", "\\1", key_value_pairs)  # Extract key
  values <- gsub(".*?:\\s*\"?(.*)\"?", "\\1", key_value_pairs)  # Extract value
  
  # Return as a named list (key-value pairs)
  return(setNames(values, keys))
}

# Apply the extraction function to each text string
extracted_data <- lapply(res_ex$answer, function(x) {
  tryCatch({
    extract_info(x)
  }, error = function(e) {
    NULL  # Return NULL if an error occurs
  })
})

# Convert the list to a data frame
extracted_df <- do.call(rbind, lapply(extracted_data, function(x) as.data.frame(t(x))))

# Function to clean each cell
clean_cell <- function(x) {
  x <- trimws(x)                        # Remove leading & trailing spaces
  x <- gsub("\"", "", x)                # Remove all double quotes
  x <- ifelse(tolower(x) %in% c("not specified", "", "na"), NA, x) # Convert "not specified" and empty values to NA
  return(x)
}

# Apply the cleaning function to all cells in the dataframe
extracted_df <- extracted_df %>% mutate_all(clean_cell)

final_apriori <- cbind(apriori, res_ex[2:4], extracted_df)

# Function to compute power analysis for t-test
compute_power <- function(statistical_test, effect_size, alpha_level, desired_power) {
  if (tolower(statistical_test) %in% c("t test", "t-test")) {
    result <- pwr::pwr.t.test(d = as.numeric(effect_size), sig.level = as.numeric(alpha_level), power = as.numeric(desired_power), type ="two.sample", alternative = "two.sided")
    sample_size <- 2*ceiling(result$n)
    return(sample_size)  # Store the sample size required
  } else {
    return(NA)  # If not a t-test, return NA
  }
}

# Apply function row-wise
final_apriori <- final_apriori %>%
  mutate(reproduced_power = pmap_dbl(
    list(statistical_test, effect_size, alpha_level, desired_power),
    compute_power
  ))

# View the result
print(final_apriori)
